findings.title: Device limit check is racy (count then insert)
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, exceeding the limit. In a multi-instance deployment the overshoot can be large. The limit is only approximately enforced.

findings.title: Cache is set before DB write and not cleared on failure
findings.body: tagDeviceUI puts the device key in the local cache before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs. If the call fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the key stays cached. Subsequent requests from the rejected device return nil and are authenticated as anonymous, bypassing the limit for about 29 minutes. Only the first request is rejected, so the limit is effectively unenforced for that device. The key should be set only after a successful write.

findings.title: Tagging moved from async goroutine to synchronous request path
findings.body: TagDevice now runs inline on the request context, so every uncached anonymous request pays for the extra DB count and write. The previous 2-minute timeout and panic recovery are gone. A slow DB now delays authentication, and a cancelled request context aborts tagging.

findings.title: Misleading ErrDeviceLimitReached for non-existent or expired devices
findings.body: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever zero rows are updated. The update is restricted to updated_at within the last 30 days, so a device that exists but is older also gets this error. The error is accurate for those cases, but the 'between the given times' comment is misleading.

findings.title: Limit test is narrow
findings.body: The test covers only the rejection of a new device at the limit. It does not test that an existing device can still be updated at the limit, or that expired devices are excluded from the count. There is also no test that Anonymous.Authenticate rejects when the limit is reached.
